title: maybe vibe gamedev is the game?
author: FotoRe_store
selftext:
so I've been making two little phone games with Claude for like 10 days. I can't code at all, I just talk to it, decide stuff and test on my phone.

and I noticed something kinda weird. I enjoy making it way more than playing the result.

like, I think "the race is boring in the first minute" or "what if the road is a river with pirate ships", we talk about it a bit, and then it's just there. on my phone. in my hand. sometimes same evening. for years ideas like this just stayed in my head because I had no way to make them real. now it's almost instant and honestly it's a crazy feeling. some days I made like 10 versions just because every one made me want to try the next thing.

when I play the finished game I mostly remember how it came together. the first time the ship actually followed my hand, or picking one of three sketches for a new world.

anyone else like this? do you even play your own games after, or is making them the real fun?

comments.author: joseph2883
comments.body: I’ve made 3 game prototypes. 1 is legit fun, 1 could be fun and looks adorable, 1 is a trash mess.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: lol same ratio here. i tried like 5 prototypes, slalom, a bomb catcher, a cave thing, arkanoid... most were trash and only 2 survived. but making the trash ones was still fun honestly

replies.author: DudeWithASweater
replies.body: I think I learn the most from my trash mess prototypes. I learn what makes it bad, why it didn't work, what could have been better, what not to do, etc

comments.author: Tom_Baron
comments.body:
the first two games I made solely because I wanted to see if I could, the first game was genuinely fun. I made it for a friday morning finance social call in work. I and my colleagues still play it. the second game I abandoned after the earliest POC because what was a good idea in my head was trash In reality.

  
So when I got the idea for the third game, I built the inner most fundamental idea first and asked myself "does it make me feel how the idea plays out in my head?" and "is there enough in this idea to build a game from it?"

And it did. 

However, I prefer watching a sim of the NPCs im using to develop and hone core gameplay features than playing myself currently. Seeing how the game develops, where stressors appear on each side, bottlenecks, rate of progress and modifying behaviour to examine advantageous strategies.   
  
Why? Because my game is still untuned, imbalanced, my UI is an early iteration, I cant get a grasp on the game from it, its saturated and unintuitive. Also, this a strategic multiplayer game rewarding cooperation and I have no one but crazy untuned NPCs to cooperate with!

  
Will I absolutely love to jump in a 48vs48 battle with a load of strangers when its tuned, balanced and complete. Yes yes yes, im looking forward to that time 😄

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: haha the "good idea in my head was trash in reality" part is so true. i had an arkanoid prototype that felt amazing in my head and was just jittery in reality, turns out a hand waiting in the air shakes by itself. and same with bots, for my race claude made bot drivers that play hundreds of races so i can see if its too hard. sometimes i watched the bot numbers more than i played myself lol. good luck with the 48vs48, sounds huge

comments.author: Aineisa
comments.body: Even before AI making games was a hobby for some.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: true! for me the code was always the wall, i had ideas but couldnt build anything. now the wall is gone and the hobby part finally works for me too

replies.author: Delyzr
replies.body: For me it was (and kind of still is) artwork. Coding was never the problem. I always found coding the easy part. Ofcourse with AI it goes 100x faster.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: funny, i had the opposite wall. for art i ended up with everything drawn by code, no images at all. it looks more simple but at least its consistent and i can change any colour in one message

replies.author: moo_sweden
replies.body: Yeah. And enjoying making levels in-game is something in between

comments.author: That1guy4226
comments.body: Exactly this. I just published my first game. I had a ton of fun making it and learned quite a lot from putting it out.   I was making a subway surfer clone for my sone to play and while figuring out background decor it kinda just popped in my head. Being able to quickly make a demo of pretty much whatever happens to come to mind on a whim has been amazing.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: congrats on publishing! the "while doing one thing another idea pops up" part is so real. half my ideas came like that, i'd be fixing something small and suddenly want a whole new world for the game. how did your son like it?

replies.author: That1guy4226
replies.body: He enjoyed the clone I made him but my actual game is a bit to complex for him. It's the old pipe screensaver turned into a 3d snake like game.

comments.author: Outrageous-Issue9722
comments.body: It is a lot of fun. That's the whole point for many of us!

comments.author: geddy
comments.body: I only got into AI game dev recently but mostly I made a few games that reminded me of the [Newgrounds.com](http://Newgrounds.com) days, small gimicky games. Things like a hot dog cart manager, a game where you solder two wires together, goofy stuff like that. It was fun but my current project is a long-term one with so much fine tuning and it's the most fun to work on yet. Granted I also love playing it so it's fun to work on AND fun to test.

comments.author: AfternoonShot9285
comments.body: It would be fun to mass assemble the vibe coders and make some game

comments.author: Maple-Syrup89
comments.body: I had 15 years of ideas I previously couldn't code. Now I can try things, discover whats fun and continue those projects. Not really the same thing, but its ok if you realize a concept isn't fun, and its ok if you realize the journey is more fun for you than the outcome. you just won't really make it as a game dev that way, if you wanted to make money, since outcome is all that matters.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body:
agree about the money part, if you want to sell then yes the outcome is what counts. but i think the outcome gets its meaning from the process. a game that nobody filled with meaning while making it usually feels empty, even if it works fine. for me the best moments are when my idea and something claude suggests suddenly click into a thing neither of us had at the start. like the idea wasnt in my head or in the ai, it was born somewhere in between. i wouldnt trade that feeling for any sales number

ps

i actually wrote a book about this kind of stuff, that meaning is more in how you live the process than in the goal

replies.author: Maple-Syrup89
replies.body:
I agree it has to be the intersection of personal meaning and humanity, and a good execution that make something special. 

One without the other is either a polished soulless terd, or a under executed piece of hot trash.

The intersection is rare, and those games, when discovered, are the ones that blow up. 

AI can help us talk to ourselves, and reveal the personal meaning and draw out our creativity. What it really does well is helps technical execution and lifts that side of the equation up. It can't be purely a crutch though.  I'm sure we both have seen dozens and dozens of soulless clones that never had the spark of meaning put into them.

replies.author: FotoRe_store
replies.body: yes the "talk to ourselves" part is exactly it for me. half the time when i discuss an idea with claude i find out what i actually wanted, it works almost like a mirror. the code is the easy part now, the spark still has to come from you. nice talk btw

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: If the game isn't fun enough to make me play after, then I haven't done a good enough job imo. The process can still be fun, but I'd chock that up as a failure --- one I can hopefully learn from. I think it's impossible to make good games people will want to play if the end result doesn't even appeal to the person developing them. This is why you should stick to genres that resonate with you and that you'd play in your spare time regardless. There can be an exception here for someone making games for their kid or someone close to them. Having that immediate feedback from them to help guide the process can make up for a lack of clear endgame for the developer themselves. But then the other person kind of becomes the director and driving force and you become their advocate to the AI for seeing their whims given life.
